{{short description|1 minus the cosine of an angle}}
{{Redir|Versin|the Polish village|Versin (village)}}
{{Trigonometry}}
{{wikt | versine | versed sine}}

The '''versine''' or '''versed sine''' is a [[trigonometric function]] found in some of the earliest ([[Sanskrit]] [[Āryabhaṭa's sine table | ''Aryabhatiya'']],<ref>
[https://archive.org/stream/The_Aryabhatiya_of_Aryabhata_Clark_1930#page/n1/mode/2up The Āryabhaṭīya by Āryabhaṭa]
</ref>
Section I) [[trigonometric table]]s. The versine of an angle is 1 minus its [[cosine]].

There are several related functions, most notably the '''coversine''' and '''haversine'''. The latter, half a versine, is of particular importance in the [[haversine formula]] of navigation.

[[Image:Unit-circle sin cos tan cot exsec excsc versin cvs.svg|thumb|190px|A [[unit circle]] with [[trigonometric function]]s.<ref name="Haslett_1855"/>]]

==<span class="anchor" id="ver"></span><span class="anchor" id="vcs"></span><span class="anchor" id="cvs"></span><span class="anchor" id="cvc"></span><span class="anchor" id="hav"></span><span class="anchor" id="hvc"></span><span class="anchor" id="hcv"></span><span class="anchor" id="hcc"></span><span class="anchor" id="lhav"></span>Overview==
<!--"cosiv" redirects here-->
The '''versine'''<ref name="Inman_1835"/><ref name="Abramowitz_1972"/><ref name="Tapson_2004"/><ref name="Atlas_2009"/><ref name="Beebe_2017"/> or '''versed sine'''<ref name="Hall_1909"/><ref name="Clagett_1969"/><ref name="Precalc_1999"/><ref name="Korn_2000"/><ref name="Calvert_2004"/> is a [[trigonometric function]] already appearing in some of the earliest trigonometric tables. It is symbolized in formulas using the abbreviations {{math|versin}}, {{math|sinver}},<ref name="Braunmühl_1903"/><ref name="Cajori_1929"/> {{math|vers}}, or {{math|siv}}.<ref name="Cauchy_1821" /><ref name="Bradley_2009" /> In [[Latin]], it is known as the {{lang|la|sinus versus}} (flipped sine), {{lang|la|versinus}}, {{lang|la|versus}}, or {{lang|la|sagitta}} (arrow).<ref name="Brummelen_2013"/>

Expressed in terms of common [[trigonometric functions]] sine, cosine, and tangent, the versine is equal to
<math display="block">
\operatorname{versin}\theta = 1 - \cos \theta = 2\sin^{2}\frac\theta2 = \sin\theta\,\tan\frac\theta2
</math>

There are several related functions corresponding to the versine:

* The '''versed cosine''',<ref name="Weisstein_vercos"/><ref group="nb" name="vercosine vs. coversine"/> or '''vercosine''', abbreviated {{math|vercosin}}, {{math|vercos}}, or {{math|vcs}}
* The '''coversed sine''' or '''coversine'''<ref name="Weisstein_covers"/> (in Latin, {{lang|la|cosinus versus}} or {{lang|la|coversinus}}), abbreviated {{math|coversin}}, {{math|covers}},<ref name="Ludlow_1891"/><ref name="Wentworth_1903"/><ref name="Kenyon_1913"/> {{math|cosiv}}, or {{math|cvs}}<ref name="Anderegg_1896"/>

Special tables were also made of half of the versed sine, because of its particular use in the [[haversine formula]] used historically in [[navigation]].

* The '''haversed sine'''<ref name="Weisstein_hav"/> or '''haversine''' ({{langx|la|semiversus|links=no}}),<ref name="Fulst_1972"/><ref name="Sauer_2015"/> abbreviated {{math|haversin}}, {{math|semiversin}}, {{math|semiversinus}}, {{math|havers}}, {{math|hav}},<ref name="Rider_1923"/><ref name="Wolfram_hav"/> {{math|hvs}},<ref group="nb" name="hvs"/> {{math|sem}}, or {{math|hv}}.<ref name="Rudzinski_2015"/> It is defined as<!--
--><math display="block">
\operatorname{hav} \theta = \sin^2 \left( \frac \theta 2 \right) = \frac {1 - \cos \theta} {2}
</math>

==History and applications==

===Versine and coversine===
[[Image:Versine.svg|right|thumb|Sine, cosine, and versine of angle {{mvar|&theta;}} in terms of a [[unit circle]] with radius 1, centered at {{mvar|O}}. This figure also illustrates the reason why the versine was sometimes called the {{lang|la|sagitta}}, Latin for [[arrow]].<ref name="Brummelen_2013"/><ref name="OED_Sagitta"/> If the arc {{mvar|ADB}} of the double-angle {{math|1=''&Delta;''&nbsp;= 2''&theta;''}} is viewed as a "[[bow (weapon)|bow]]" and the [[Chord (geometry)|chord]] {{mvar|AB}} as its "string", then the versine {{mvar|CD}} is clearly the "arrow shaft".]]
[[File:historical_trigonometric_functions_graph.svg|thumb|250px|link={{filepath:historical_trigonometric_functions_graph.svg}}|Graphs of historical trigonometric functions compared with sin and cos &ndash; in [[:Media:historical_trigonometric_functions_graph.svg|the SVG file]], hover over or click a graph to highlight it]]
The ordinary ''[[sine]]'' function ([[Sine and cosine#Etymology|see note on etymology]]) was sometimes historically called the {{lang|la|sinus rectus}} ("straight sine"), to contrast it with the versed sine ({{lang|la|sinus versus}}).<ref name="Boyer_1991"/> The meaning of these terms is apparent if one looks at the functions in the original context for their definition, a [[unit circle]]:

For a vertical [[Chord (geometry)|chord]] {{mvar|AB}} of the unit circle, the sine of the angle {{mvar|&theta;}} (representing half of the subtended angle {{mvar|&Delta;}}) is the distance {{mvar|AC}} (half of the chord). On the other hand, the versed sine of {{mvar|&theta;}} is the distance {{mvar|CD}} from the center of the chord to the center of the arc. Thus, the sum of {{math|cos(''&theta;'')}} (equal to the length of line {{mvar|OC}}) and {{math|versin(''&theta;'')}} (equal to the length of line {{mvar|CD}}) is the radius {{mvar|OD}} (with length 1). Illustrated this way, the sine is vertical ({{lang|la|rectus}}, literally "straight") while the versine is horizontal ({{lang|la|versus}}, literally "turned against, out-of-place"); both are distances from {{mvar|C}} to the circle.

This figure also illustrates the reason why the versine was sometimes called the {{lang|la|sagitta}}, Latin for [[arrow]].<ref name="Brummelen_2013"/><ref name="OED_Sagitta"/> If the arc {{mvar|ADB}} of the double-angle {{math|1=''&Delta;''&nbsp;= 2''&theta;''}} is viewed as a "[[bow (weapon)|bow]]" and the chord {{mvar|AB}} as its "string", then the versine {{mvar|CD}} is clearly the "arrow shaft".

In further keeping with the interpretation of the sine as "vertical" and the versed sine as "horizontal", {{lang|la|sagitta}} is also an obsolete synonym for the [[abscissa]] (the horizontal axis of a graph).<ref name="OED_Sagitta"/>

In 1821, [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy|Cauchy]] used the terms {{lang|la|sinus versus}} (''siv'') for the versine and {{lang|la|cosinus versus}} (''cosiv'') for the coversine.<ref name="Cauchy_1821"/><ref name="Bradley_2009"/><ref group="nb" name="vercosine vs. coversine"/>

[[Image:Unit-circle_sin_cos_tan_cot_exsec_excsc_versin_vercos_coversin_covercos.svg|right|thumb|320px|The trigonometric functions can be constructed geometrically in terms of a [[unit circle]] centered at {{mvar|O}}.]]

As {{mvar|&theta;}} goes to zero, {{math|versin(''&theta;'')}} is the difference between two nearly equal quantities, so a user of a [[trigonometric table]] for the cosine alone would need a very high accuracy to obtain the versine in order to avoid [[catastrophic cancellation]], making separate tables for the latter convenient.<ref name="Calvert_2004"/> Even with a calculator or computer, [[round-off error]]s make it advisable to use the {{math|sin<sup>2</sup>}} formula for small&nbsp;{{mvar|&theta;}}.

Another historical advantage of the versine is that it is always non-negative, so its [[logarithm]] is defined everywhere except for the single angle ({{math|1=''&theta;'' = 0, 2{{pi}}, ...}}) where it is zero&mdash;thus, one could use [[logarithmic table]]s for multiplications in formulas involving versines.

In fact, the earliest surviving table of sine (half-[[Chord (geometry)|chord]]) values (as opposed to the [[Ptolemy's table of chords|chords tabulated by Ptolemy]] and other Greek authors), calculated from the [[Surya Siddhanta|Surya Siddhantha]] of India dated back to the 3rd century BC, was a table of values for the sine and versed sine (in {{math|3.75°}} increments from {{math|0}} to {{math|90°}}).<ref name="Boyer_1991"/>

The versine appears as an intermediate step in the application of the [[half-angle formula]] {{math|1=sin<sup>2</sup>{{big|(}}{{sfrac|''θ''|2}}{{big|)}} = {{sfrac|1|2}}versin(''&theta;'')}}, derived by [[Ptolemy]], that was used to construct such tables.

===Haversine===
The haversine, in particular, was important in [[navigation]] because it appears in the [[haversine formula]], which is used to reasonably accurately compute distances on an astronomic [[spheroid]] (see issues with the [[equatorial bulge|Earth's radius vs. sphere]]) given angular positions (e.g., [[longitude]] and [[latitude]]). One could also use {{math|sin<sup>2</sup>{{big|(}}{{sfrac|''θ''|2}}{{big|)}}}} directly, but having a table of the haversine removed the need to compute squares and square roots.<ref name="Calvert_2004"/>

An early utilization by [[José de Mendoza y Ríos]] of what later would be called haversines is documented in 1801.<!-- [[Law of haversines]] of spherical trigonometry, perhaps even 1795 --><ref name="Cajori_1929"/><ref name="Ríos_1795"/>

The first known English equivalent to a [[table of haversines]] was published by James Andrew in 1805, under the name "Squares of Natural Semi-Chords".<ref name="RCA_1945"/><ref name="Andrew_1805"/><ref name="Brummelen_2013"/>

In 1835,<!-- Cajori, 1929, even mentions the original 1821 issue of Inman's book, but does not state, that Inman invented the term haversine himself. --> the term ''[[haversine]]'' (notated naturally as ''hav.'' or [[base-10 logarithm]]ically as ''log. haversine'' or ''log. havers.'') was coined<ref name="OED_1989_Haversine"/> by [[James Inman]]<ref name="Cajori_1929"/><ref name="White_1926-02"/><ref name="White_1926-07"/> in the third edition of his work ''Navigation and Nautical Astronomy: For the Use of British Seamen'' to simplify the calculation of distances between two points on the surface of the Earth using [[spherical trigonometry]] for applications in navigation.<ref name="Inman_1835"/><ref name="OED_1989_Haversine"/> Inman also used the terms ''nat.<!-- natural --> versine'' and ''nat.<!-- natural --> vers.'' for versines.<ref name="Inman_1835"/>

Other high-regarded tables of haversines were those of Richard Farley in 1856<ref name="RCA_1945"/><ref name="Farley_1856"/> and John Caulfield Hannyngton in 1876.<ref name="RCA_1945"/><ref name="Hannyngton_1876"/>

The haversine continues to be used in navigation and has found new applications in recent decades, as in Bruce D. Stark's method for clearing [[lunar distance (navigation)|lunar distance]]s utilizing [[Gaussian logarithm]]s since 1995<ref name="Stark_1997"/><ref name="Kalivoda_2003"/> or in a more compact method for [[sight reduction]] since 2014.<ref name="Rudzinski_2015"/>

===Modern uses===
While the usage of the versine, coversine and haversine as well as their [[#Inverse functions|inverse function]]s can be traced back centuries, the names for the other five [[cofunction]]s appear to be of much younger origin.

One period ({{math|0 < ''&theta;'' < 2''&pi;''}}) of a versine or, more commonly, a haversine waveform is also commonly used in [[signal processing]] and [[control theory]] as the shape of a [[pulse (signal processing)|pulse]] or a [[window function]] (including [[Hann window|Hann]], [[Hann–Poisson window|Hann–Poisson]] and [[Tukey window]]s), because it smoothly ([[continuous function|continuous]] in value and [[slope]]) "turns on" from [[0 (number)|zero]] to [[1 (number)|one]] (for haversine) and back to zero.<ref group="nb" name="hvs"/> In these applications, it is named [[Hann function]] or [[raised-cosine filter]].

==Mathematical identities==

===Definitions===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
| <math>\operatorname{versin} (\theta) := 2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = 1 - \cos (\theta) \,</math><ref name="Abramowitz_1972"/>
|| [[File:Versin plot 2.svg|300px|Plot of versin]]
|-
| <math>\operatorname{coversin}(\theta) := \operatorname{versin}\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = 1 - \sin(\theta) \,</math><ref name="Abramowitz_1972"/>
|| [[File:Coversin plot 2.svg|300px|Plot of coversin]]
|-
| <math>\operatorname{vercosin} (\theta) := 2\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = 1 + \cos (\theta) \,</math><ref name="Weisstein_vercos"/>
|| [[File:Vercosin plot 2.svg|300px|Plot of vercosin]]
|-
| <math>\operatorname{haversin}(\theta) := \frac {\operatorname{versin}(\theta)} {2} = \sin^2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{1 - \cos (\theta)}{2} \,</math><ref name="Abramowitz_1972"/>
|| [[File:Haversin plot 2.svg|300px|Plot of haversin]]
|}

===Circular rotations===
The functions are circular rotations of each other.
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \operatorname{versin}(\theta)
    &= \operatorname{coversin}\left(\theta + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)
     = \operatorname{vercosin}\left(\theta + \pi\right) 
\end{align}</math>

===Derivatives and integrals===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
|  <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\operatorname{versin}(x) = \sin{x}</math><ref name="Weisstein_vers"/>
|| <math>\int\operatorname{versin}(x) \,\mathrm{d}x = x - \sin{x} + C</math><ref name="Abramowitz_1972"/><ref name="Weisstein_vers"/>
|-
|  <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\operatorname{vercosin}(x) = -\sin{x}</math>
|| <math>\int\operatorname{vercosin}(x) \,\mathrm{d}x = x + \sin{x} + C</math>
|-
|  <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\operatorname{coversin}(x) = -\cos{x}</math><ref name="Weisstein_covers"/>
|| <math>\int\operatorname{coversin}(x) \,\mathrm{d}x = x + \cos{x} + C</math><ref name="Weisstein_covers"/>
|-
|  <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\operatorname{haversin}(x) = \frac{\sin{x}}{2}</math><ref name="Weisstein_hav"/>
|| <math>\int\operatorname{haversin}(x) \,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{x - \sin{x}}{2} + C</math><ref name="Weisstein_hav"/>
|}

===<span class="anchor" id="aver"></span><span class="anchor" id="avcs"></span><span class="anchor" id="acvs"></span><span class="anchor" id="acvc"></span><span class="anchor" id="ahav"></span><span class="anchor" id="ahvc"></span><span class="anchor" id="ahcv"></span><span class="anchor" id="ahcc"></span>Inverse functions===
Inverse functions like '''arcversine''' (arcversin, arcvers,<ref name="Hall_1909"/> avers,<ref name="Simpson_2001"/><ref name="Doel_2010"/> aver), '''arcvercosine''' (arcvercosin, arcvercos, avercos, avcs), '''arccoversine''' (arccoversin, arccovers,<ref name="Hall_1909"/> acovers,<ref name="Simpson_2001"/><ref name="Doel_2010"/> acvs), '''arccovercosine''' (arccovercosin, arccovercos, acovercos, acvc), '''archaversine''' (archaversin, archav, haversin<sup>−1</sup>,<ref name="Plus_hav"/> invhav,<ref name="Skvarc_1999"/><ref name="Skvarc_2014"/><ref name="Ballew_2007"/> ahav,<ref name="Simpson_2001"/><ref name="Doel_2010"/> ahvs, ahv, hav<sup>−1</sup><ref name="Weisstein_ahav"/><ref name="Wolfram_ahav"/>), '''archavercosine''' (archavercosin, archavercos, ahvc), '''archacoversine''' (archacoversin, ahcv) or '''archacovercosine''' (archacovercosin, archacovercos, ahcc) exist as well:

{| class="wikitable"
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{arcversin}(y) = \arccos\left(1-y\right)\,</math><ref name="Simpson_2001"/><ref name="Doel_2010"/>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{arcvercos}(y) = \arccos\left(y-1\right)\,</math>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{arccoversin}(y) = \arcsin\left(1-y\right)\,</math><ref name="Simpson_2001"/><ref name="Doel_2010"/>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{arccovercos}(y) = \arcsin\left(y-1\right)\,</math>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{archaversin}(y) = 2\arcsin\left(\sqrt{y}\right) = \arccos\left(1-2y\right)\,</math><ref name="Simpson_2001"/><ref name="Doel_2010"/><ref name="Plus_hav"/><ref name="Skvarc_1999"/><ref name="Skvarc_2014"/><ref name="Weisstein_ahav"/><ref name="Wolfram_ahav"/>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{archavercos}(y) = 2\arccos\left(\sqrt{y}\right) = \arccos\left(2y-1\right)</math>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{archacoversin}(y) = \arcsin\left(1-2y\right)\,</math>
|-
|| <math>\operatorname{archacovercos}(y) = \arcsin\left(2y-1\right)\,</math>
|}

===Other properties===
These functions can be extended into the [[complex plane]].<ref name="Weisstein_vers"/><ref name="Weisstein_covers"/><ref name="Weisstein_hav"/>

[[Maclaurin series]]:<ref name="Weisstein_hav"/>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    \operatorname{versin}(z) &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1} z^{2k}}{(2k)!} \\
  \operatorname{haversin}(z) &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1} z^{2k}}{2(2k)!}
\end{align}</math>

<math>\lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{\operatorname{versin}(\theta)}{\theta} = 0</math><ref name="Hall_1909"/>

<math>\begin{align}
  \frac{\operatorname{versin}(\theta) + \operatorname{coversin}(\theta)}
       {\operatorname{versin}(\theta) - \operatorname{coversin}(\theta)} -
  \frac{\operatorname{exsec}(\theta) + \operatorname{excsc}(\theta)}
       {\operatorname{exsec}(\theta) - \operatorname{excsc}(\theta)}
    &= \frac{2 \operatorname{versin}(\theta) \operatorname{coversin}(\theta)}
            {\operatorname{versin}(\theta) - \operatorname{coversin}(\theta)} \\[3pt]
  [\operatorname{versin}(\theta) + \operatorname{exsec}(\theta)]\,
       [\operatorname{coversin}(\theta) + \operatorname{excsc}(\theta)]
    &= \sin(\theta) \cos(\theta)
\end{align}</math><ref name="Hall_1909"/>

==Approximations==
[[File:Comparison of Versine Approximations for Angles of 0 to 2 Pi.svg|thumb|Comparison of the versine function with three approximations to the versine functions, for angles ranging from {{math|0}} to {{math|2''π''}}]]

[[File:Comparison of Versine Approximations for Angles of 0 to Pi divided by 2.svg|thumb|Comparison of the versine function with three approximations to the versine functions, for angles ranging from {{math|0}} to {{math|''π''/2}}]]

When the versine {{mvar|v}} is small in comparison to the radius {{mvar|r}}, it may be approximated from the half-chord length {{mvar|L}} (the distance {{mvar|AC}} shown above) by the formula<ref name="Woodward_1978"/>
<math display="block">v \approx \frac{L^2}{2r}.</math>

Alternatively, if the versine is small and the versine, radius, and half-chord length are known, they may be used to estimate the arc length {{mvar|s}} ({{mvar|AD}} in the figure above) by the formula
<math display="block">s\approx L+\frac{v^2}{r}</math>
This formula was known to the Chinese mathematician [[Shen Kuo]], and a more accurate formula also involving the sagitta was developed two centuries later by [[Guo Shoujing]].<ref name="Needham_1959"/>

A more accurate approximation used in engineering<ref name="Boardman_1930"/> is
<math display="block">v\approx \frac{s^\frac{3}{2} L^\frac{1}{2}}{8r}</math>

==Arbitrary curves and chords==
The term ''versine'' is also sometimes used to describe deviations from straightness in an arbitrary planar curve, of which the above circle is a special case. Given a chord between two points in a curve, the perpendicular distance {{mvar|v}} from the chord to the curve (usually at the chord midpoint) is called a ''versine'' measurement. For a straight line, the versine of any chord is zero, so this measurement characterizes the straightness of the curve. In the [[limit (mathematics)|limit]] as the chord length {{mvar|L}} goes to zero, the ratio {{math|{{sfrac|8''v''|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}}} goes to the instantaneous [[curvature]]. This usage is especially common in [[rail transport]], where it describes measurements of the straightness of the [[rail tracks]]<ref name="Nair_1972"/> and it is the basis of the [[Hallade method]] for [[rail surveying]].

The term ''[[sagitta (optics)|sagitta]]'' (often abbreviated ''sag'') is used similarly in [[optics]], for describing the surfaces of [[lens (optics)|lens]]es and [[mirror]]s.

==Notes==
{{reflist|group="nb"|refs=
<ref group="nb" name="vercosine vs. coversine">{{anchor|Bradley-Errata|Korn-Errata}}Some English sources confuse the versed cosine with the coversed sine. Historically (f.e. in [[#Cauchy-1821|Cauchy, 1821]]), the {{lang|la|sinus versus}} (versine) was defined as {{math|1=siv(''&theta;'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 − cos(''&theta;'')}}, the {{lang|la|cosinus versus}} (what is now also known as coversine) as {{math|1=cosiv(''&theta;'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 − sin(''&theta;'')}}, and the vercosine as {{math|1=vcs ''&theta;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 + cos(''&theta;'')}}. However, in their 2009 English translation of Cauchy's work, [[#Bradley-2009|Bradley and Sandifer]] associate the {{lang|la|cosinus versus}} (and cosiv) with the ''versed cosine'' (what is now also known as vercosine) rather than the ''coversed sine''. Similarly, in their 1968/2000 work, [[#Korn-2000|Korn and Korn]] associate the {{math|covers(''&theta;'')}} function with the ''versed cosine'' instead of the ''coversed sine''.</ref>
<ref group="nb" name="hvs">The abbreviation ''hvs'' sometimes used for the haversine function in signal processing and filtering is also sometimes used for the unrelated [[Heaviside step function]].</ref>
}}
